prompt: Some schools have replaced letter grades with written feedback only. Write an essay arguing whether this is a good idea.
text:
# Feedback Without Letters: A Good Idea, Done Carefully

Some schools have dropped letter grades and now give students only written feedback. The change sounds gentle, even obvious. A paragraph of comments seems to say more than a "B+" ever could. I think the idea is sound in principle, but it works only when schools handle its costs honestly. Used carelessly, it can leave students and families knowing less than before.

## What letter grades do badly

A letter grade compresses a lot of information into one symbol. A "B" might mean a student understood the material but made careless errors. It might mean she mastered half the course and missed the rest. It might mean he turned in every assignment on time but struggled on tests. The student sees the same letter in each case and has no idea what to do next.

Grades also change what students care about. Once a mark is attached to every task, many students start asking "What do I need to get an A?" rather than "What do I need to understand?" Research on motivation, including studies by Ruth Butler in the 1980s, found that students who received only grades, or grades with comments, showed less interest and improved less than students who received comments alone. The grade tends to draw attention away from the advice. Students glance at the letter and skip the explanation.

Grades can also discourage risk. A student who fears a bad mark will choose the easy essay topic and avoid the hard problem. Learning often requires attempting things you might fail at, and grades make failure expensive.

## What written feedback does well

Good written feedback tells a student what she did well, where she went wrong, and what to try next. It treats her as someone who can improve, not someone being sorted. It also gives teachers a reason to look closely at each student's thinking, which can improve their teaching.

Feedback-only systems also reduce some of the pressure that harms students' well-being. A student who stumbles early in a course is not branded with a low mark that stays in the average. She can revise, try again, and show growth.

## The real problems

The critics have fair points, and they deserve straight answers.

**Teacher workload.** Writing thoughtful comments for 150 students takes far more time than assigning letters. If schools adopt the policy without cutting class sizes or giving teachers more time, the comments will become vague and repetitive ("Good effort, keep it up"). That is worse than a grade, because it looks like information but contains none.

**Inconsistency.** Teachers vary in how they write. One may be blunt and another very gentle. A parent comparing two reports may not know which student is doing better. Grades are crude, but they are at least a shared scale.

**Outside demands.** Colleges, scholarships, and employers often want a simple measure. Schools that drop grades usually have to convert their comments into something comparable anyway, or send admissions offices long narrative reports that few people have time to read. Students from schools without grades can be disadvantaged if the receiving institution does not know how to interpret their records.

**Hidden inequality.** Written feedback is only as useful as the student's ability to read and act on it. Students with more support at home may get more from it. Vague comments can also hide teacher bias more easily than a number can, because there is nothing concrete to compare or challenge.

## What makes it work

The best versions of this approach do not simply delete the letter and leave a blank. They replace it with something clearer. Three features matter most:

1. **Clear criteria.** Teachers should state in advance what success looks like, and comments should refer to those standards. This keeps feedback specific and keeps it fair across classrooms.
2. **Time and training.** Schools must give teachers the hours and the skills to write useful feedback, or the system will fail in practice.
3. **A plan for the outside world.** Schools need a way to give colleges and employers a readable summary, such as a short competency record, without bringing back the daily pressure of grades.

## Conclusion

Letter grades are convenient, but convenience is not the same as usefulness. They flatten what a student knows, push learners toward chasing marks, and often go unexplained. Written feedback addresses those flaws and supports real improvement. But it asks more of teachers, and it can confuse families and institutions that are used to a simple scale.

So my answer is yes, with conditions. Schools should replace letter grades with written feedback only if they commit the time, the training, and the clear standards that make the comments meaningful. Without that support, removing grades is just a way of hiding the problem. With it, schools can finally give students what grades promised but rarely delivered: an honest picture of what they know and how to get better.
